comment_content:
The broader context makes the failure worse. Higher education faces legitimate criticism about cost, relevance, and declining standards. Courses like this supply the critics with evidence. When a professor treats class time as a personal platform and reduces the curriculum to unreadable slides, he is not merely disappointing a room full of students. He is contributing to the erosion of trust in the institution itself. Students leave such courses cynical. They learn that the formal structure of education can be hollow, that credentials can be awarded without corresponding instruction, and that some faculty view teaching as secondary to whatever private interests currently hold their attention. That lesson is more lasting, and more damaging, than any of the actual course content.
It is possible to imagine a version of this course that works. The same material, delivered by an instructor who prioritizes explanation over self-reference, who designs slides that illuminate rather than overwhelm, who treats class time as a scarce resource to be used for the students’ benefit rather than his own amusement, would be unremarkable in the best sense: solid, useful, respectful of the students’ time and money. The gap between that hypothetical course and the one actually offered is the measure of the failure. The professor does not teach the course content. He yaps about his AI chatbot and other bullshit. The slides are long paragraphs. The semester is a lost opportunity. Students deserve better. The subject deserves better. And any institution that tolerates this level of instructional neglect should be embarrassed.
comment_teaching:
There are courses that challenge you. There are courses that frustrate you in productive ways. And then there are courses that make you question the entire premise of higher education, the value of your tuition dollars, and the basic competence of the person standing at the front of the room. This course belongs firmly in the last category. It is not merely mediocre. It is actively corrosive to the learning process. The professor does not teach. He does not facilitate understanding. He does not even attempt to make the material accessible. Instead, he treats the classroom as a personal stage for monologues about his AI chatbot and a parade of other irrelevant tangents, while the actual course content is reduced to dense, unbroken walls of text dumped onto PowerPoint slides. What follows is not a polite student evaluation. It is an indictment.
Let us begin with the most glaring failure: the professor does not teach the course content. Teaching, in any meaningful sense, requires structure, explanation, scaffolding, and engagement with the material students are expected to master. None of that happens here. Class sessions are not lectures on the syllabus topics. They are free-associative performances in which the professor drifts, at length and with evident self-satisfaction, into extended commentary about his AI chatbot. He will spend twenty minutes describing how the bot responds to certain prompts, how he has fine-tuned it, how it generates surprising outputs, how it might one day replace certain professional tasks. Students sit there, notebooks open or laptops ready, waiting for any connection to the week’s readings, the assigned theories, the concepts listed in the course outline. The connection never arrives. The chatbot is not an illustration of a course concept. It is not a case study. It is simply the thing the professor finds interesting that day, and the classroom exists to host his interest.
This is not occasional digression. It is the dominant mode. On days when the chatbot is not the star, the professor substitutes other forms of bullshit. Personal anecdotes that go nowhere. Opinions about unrelated campus politics. Long asides about technology trends that have nothing to do with the stated learning objectives. Rhetorical questions that he answers himself at length. The pattern is consistent: the actual subject of the course is treated as an inconvenience that must be briefly acknowledged before the real business of talking about whatever occupies the professor’s mind can resume. Students who try to steer the conversation back to the material are met with polite deflection or, more often, simply ignored as the monologue continues. The result is a semester in which large stretches of class time are consumed by content that will never appear on any assessment and that contributes nothing to understanding the field.
When the professor does deign to address the course material, the method of delivery is almost comically inadequate. The PowerPoint slides are not teaching tools. They are dumping grounds. Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense prose are copied or lightly paraphrased onto slides, often in small font, with minimal visual hierarchy, no diagrams that actually clarify relationships, no progressive disclosure of ideas, and no attempt to highlight key claims or distinguish primary arguments from supporting detail. A single slide may contain an entire page of textbook-style text. Students are expected to read this while the professor either reads it aloud in a monotone or, more commonly, ignores it entirely while returning to his preferred topics. The slides do not support learning; they actively obstruct it. Cognitive science has established for decades that people cannot effectively process dense text while simultaneously listening to a speaker. The design of these materials violates every basic principle of instructional design. They are not slides. They are poorly formatted handouts projected onto a wall.
The cumulative effect on students is predictable and damaging. Motivation collapses. Why prepare for class when class will not engage the preparation? Why struggle with difficult concepts when the person responsible for guiding that struggle is instead describing chatbot outputs? Attendance becomes a performative exercise rather than a learning opportunity. Students who care about the subject are forced into a double workload: they must teach themselves the material outside of class while also enduring the opportunity cost of sitting through sessions that add nothing. Those who are less intrinsically motivated simply disengage, collect whatever grade the assessments allow, and leave with the accurate impression that the course was a waste of time. The assessments themselves often feel disconnected from what happened in the room, because what happened in the room had so little to do with the content. Students are graded on material the professor never meaningfully taught.
This is not a matter of teaching style. Different styles can be effective. Some professors lecture tightly. Some facilitate discussion. Some use cases, problems, or demonstrations. What is not a legitimate style is the systematic refusal to engage the subject matter in favor of personal preoccupations, paired with presentation materials that treat students as readers of projected walls of text rather than learners who need guidance. The AI chatbot fixation is particularly revealing. It suggests a professor more interested in signaling proximity to a trendy technology than in developing competence in the domain he is paid to teach. The chatbot becomes a form of academic performance art: look at me, engaging with the future, while the present responsibility of instruction goes unmet.
One might object that students should simply read the slides and the assigned materials and succeed independently. That objection concedes the point. If the classroom adds so little value that independent reading is the only reliable path to learning, then the course has already failed as a taught experience. Universities do not charge tuition for the privilege of reading dense text alone. They charge for expertise, structured guidance, intellectual modeling, and the creation of an environment in which difficult ideas become clearer through interaction with a knowledgeable instructor. None of those goods are delivered here.

comment_content:
Should you take the course?
If you have taken HKDSE Physics (esp. E3 -- Energy and Use of Energy), you must take this course! This course is just an extension of HKDSE Physics E3, covering everything in buildings. 
If you are not a science student/ have not taken HKDSE physics, you may still enrol in this course and just give it a try.
Details
A. Course Schedules
For course details, you may refer to other reviews about Prof. Ng on this course. He just grouped 2 lectures in the regular semester into 1 lecture in the summer semester, with 2 hours 50 mins long (including 10-15 mins break). 
In the final week, one lecture would be a course review covering all calculation problems, homework solutions and a case study on green buildings. While the last lecture would be the final exam.
B. Assignment
There will be a total of 5 assignments on calculation ONLY.
Assignment 1: Calculate the electricity bill for both commercial and residential consumers in Hong Kong (CLP users only).
Assignment 2: Calculate the amount of CO2 released by different public transports.
Assignment 3: Calculate the capacity factor (actual energy output/designed energy output*100%) of wind turbines.
Assignment 4: Calculate battery capacity and air fuel ratio
Assignment 5: Calculate the rate of heat flow by conduction and lighting quantities
C. Quiz
There is no mid-term exam in the summer semester. To replace it, 4 closed-book and **pop-up** quizzes were held in the last 30 mins of the lecture without prior announcement! So make sure you attend the lectures :) All quizzes are long questions with a full mark of 10.
Quiz 1: How can buildings benefit occupants?
Quiz 2: Name 5 aspects of green buildings and briefly explain.
Quiz 3: What are the differences between LPG and LNG?
Quiz 4: Draw a diagram of the system of an air conditioner and explain how an air conditioner works.
Tips: If Prof. Ng suddenly repeat the contents in the previous lectures, they will likely appear on quiz.
D. Final Exam
Full Mark: 100 marks     No. of Qs: 6
You are allowed to bring 2 A4 cheat sheets with handwriting ONLY.
2 Long Questions (20%@10%) Format similiar to quiz
Q1: Explain some methods that can control the noise produced by HVAC systems in buildings.
Q2: Describe the green features of green building materials in manufacturing, building, and their waste management stage.
4 Calculation Questions (80%@20%) Format similiar to homework
Q1: Calculate the electricity bill
Q2: Calculate the capacity factor of hydroelectric power
Q3: Calculate the power loss in the transmission line
Q4: Calculate the lighting quantities of table lights

comment_grading:
10% Attendance&Participation
The attendance policy for this course stipulates that students cannot miss more than 2 lectures to receive the full attendance mark. To earn the participation component of the grade, students must actively engage in class discussions. However, the calculation of the participation mark is ambiguous.
40% Group project
The grading is based on slides and presentations, with the assessment comprising identification and description of management issues (20%), analysis of cause (20%), generation and evaluation of alternative actions (40%), description of recommendation/implementation (10%), and presentation skills (10%).
50% Final exam
The final exam consists of 20 multiple-choice questions, 3 short answer questions, and 2 scenario analysis questions. Students are permitted to bring a double-sided A4 cheat sheet for the exam, but it is not sufficient to cover all the necessary details. With only 1 sample scenario analysis question provided beforehand, it was difficult for us to anticipate the exact content that would be covered in this portion of the exam. As a result, many students ended up including unnecessary information on their cheat sheets.
The MCs primarily test conceptual knowledge, so they are relatively manageable. However, the LQs are more challenging, as they often require providing multiple examples or applying theories to real-world problems, rather than just recalling information. This combination of question types and formats made it quite demanding to prepare thoroughly for the final exam.
Remark:
After the grades were released, I was pleasantly surprised by the final result. In my opinion, the grading was quite good, even though there were a few areas where I struggled. It's certain that I attended all the lectures, but I only participated in discussions around three times throughout the semester. 
Our group also encountered challenges with the group project, as we ended up including an excessive amount of content, which seemed to leave everyone in the class a bit confused. 
In the final exam, I didn't perform as well on the LQs, especially the last scenario analysis question. I had anticipated my overall grade would likely fall in the B range, perhaps a B or B+. However, to my pleasant surprise, I ended up earning an A in the course.

comment_content:
人對於知識的追求，源於探尋世界本質的渴望。於此，人憑藉理性之光，航向未知的深藍。但海洋之奧秘豈僅封存於冰冷數據？若真理散落於雜亂無章的碎片，若傳道者之言晦澀如迷，知識的燈塔又如何照亮求索之路？
吾等修習海洋生物及環境科學，本欲窺探碧波之下生生不息的法則。然此課之荒謬，非片語能盡述。小子未歷滄桑，僅能以殘筆數行，略陳其四宗罪。
1. 資訊洪流中的迷失。 課程文件猶如遭風暴肆虐後的殘骸，數據與圖表胡亂堆疊，關鍵資訊化為圖片邊陲的螻蟻小字，彷彿刻意隱匿於視野的荒原。求知者本應循邏輯之徑漫步，在此卻被迫於文字與圖像的迷宮中匍匐尋覓，拾撿破碎的數字殘片。此非傳道授業，此乃令學者於資訊泥沼中自生自滅。
2. 語言之獄與靈感的枯竭。 講者之口，如深潛者隔著厚重面罩發出的模糊嗡鳴，其語調之平鋪直敘，足令潮汐停息、鯨歌喑啞。更甚者，其所用之語彙與邏輯，自成一種封閉的符號系統，將課堂化為僅供其一人低語的密室。縱有萬頃碧波之奇趣，在此等講述下，亦褪色為乾涸標本上的塵埃。熱忱之火，輕易便被此等冰冷與晦澀所掐滅。
3. 權威的傲慢與對話的死亡。 此課堂奉行不容置疑的「單向真理」。教授者立於講臺，彷彿手持絕對詮釋權杖，其指點之圖文縱然雜亂無章、令人費解，亦被鍍上一層「標準答案」的金漆。任何質疑與探討的嘗試，皆遭無形壁壘彈回。知識本應在對話與辯證中奔流，在此卻凝固為必須虔誠背誦的教條。學習之目的，悄然異化為破解講者心意的猜謎遊戲，而非追索客觀真實。
4. 負擔的錯位與核心價值的悖反。 通識課程，本意乃拓寬視野、調劑心神，於繁重專業課間闢一扇眺望蒼穹的窗。然此課反其道而行，以龐雜混亂的材料與專斷封閉的氛圍，織成一張最緻密的精神負擔之網。它未曾成為歇腳的綠洲，反成了需額外耗費心神去解碼、去迎合、去勉強消化的險灘。這是一種深刻的錯置，將求知的愉悅，扭曲為順從的疲憊。
而默許此等教學存續、對學生困惑置若罔聞的體系——大學本身——實與此風氣同流共棲。二者相遇，非學子之幸，乃求真路上的一片需要艱難跋涉的無光之海。
comment_teaching:
人之授業，聲調為舟，渡學生於知識之川。若舟楫雖美，其行卻滯重如陷泥淖，則再遼闊的彼岸，亦成無法抵達的困倦遠方。
講者之音，枯燥至極，雖帶標準口音，猶如精緻棺木盛放朽骨。每當於計算機課後踏入此堂，那平穩無波的聲線，便成了催眠的咒文，令人在學習共享空間中，不自覺墜入意識的深淵。
後記：Cindy之教學，較Cynthia尤為不堪。其授課恍若夢遊，言語間盡顯對所授之物的陌生與惶惑。更令人愕然者，身為教授，其英語水平竟貧瘠如中學文憑試四級之流。學術殿堂之門檻，何時淪落至此？
綜觀二者，授業無神，懶散入骨：因懶於批改，故無作業（此點或可稱幸）；因懶於批改，故僅設選擇題；因懶於安排，故無座次規劃；因懶於檢視，故無試卷覆核。授業者怠惰至此，猶如燈塔熄火、嚮導迷途，彼等何德何能，竟坐享薪俸？此非教學，乃制度豢養之懶散，蠶食學子光陰與期許的無聲災厄。
comment_grading:
此文乃考後鬱結難平所書，積憤充膺，不吐不快。
吾曾耗三日心力，焚膏繼晷，強記課件中每一細節。然試卷一展，所考竟多為投影片邊角縫隙處之微末瑣碎。平生光陰，竟虛擲於此等無謂之事，豈不悲乎？更甚者，題意曖昧不明，吾深疑出題者自身概念混沌，誤人子弟。此等課程，諸君萬勿涉足；此等考試，實乃毫無價值、徒惹憤懣之舉。
後記：期中試平均分40.56（滿分50），標準差5.24。試期為十月十六日，而成績竟遲至十一月三日夜晚方公佈，公然違背校方「兩週內回饋成績」之政策。尤有甚者，教授姿態傲慢，令人扼腕。
其試卷設計實屬詭異。專考邊角資料已令人無奈，然若溫習純熟，更會發現卷中多項選擇之措辭粗劣不堪，充滿混淆。得分遠低於自身預期，與同儕核對後更覺差距不合常理。其後，教授於公告中輕描淡寫，稱部分題目「有多於一個答案」，已「慷慨」給予分數，卻斷然拒絕覆核查卷。矛盾之處在於：既自知試卷錯漏百出，需不斷修正答案，又何以確信自己已全然更正？不讓學生查卷、不聽取回饋，又如何得知改卷確無謬誤？此乃傲慢與無知之結合體。課堂上常聞其言：「網上資訊雖多，然我等永遠正確，故只須參考本課筆記。」原以為是戲言，豈料處理正事時竟真抱此心態。如今面對不明不白之分數，無端承受低劣等級…或可歸咎於本人平庸，然在不允許覆核的前提下，我連此點亦無法確認。唯一可肯定者，乃教授之狂妄自大，與評核過程之極度不透明。我並非斷言考試必然不公，然從我的視角觀之，此可能性確實存在。是否要以學業前途作賭注，諸君請自行決斷。
期末考紀實：
整份試卷幾乎全然超出課程綱要，多道題目所涉內容我從未見過，大量詞彙不知所云，溫習過後仍須猜測近半答案。忠告諸君：不必為期末考溫習，因其荒唐程度更甚期中——期中所考至少課堂曾有提及，期末所問則根本無跡可尋。與同窗查證後發現，此次重點不在投影片邊角，而在投影片內圖片之中——那些編排混亂、無人能解其意的圖片，其上印有極細小文字，竟成為主要考題，而我對此一無所知。請相信，無論你起初多有熱忱，在閱讀期中後（即Cindy負責部分）的投影片五分鐘內，所有動力必將熄滅。欲強記所有無謂內容實屬不可能，而將如許光陰虛耗於一門通識課程，只為背誦謬誤，更毫無價值——我曾核對網上可靠資源，發現其投影片內容實有謬誤，然他們始終強調「我等永遠正確」，學生必須遵從。是故，我們作答並非基於事實，而是基於他們自以為是的認知，研習此科根本毫無意義。此外，他們從不提供練習題目，我開始懷疑他們是否每年沿用同一試卷，並在收回試題後便可隨心所欲，更不設覆核查卷環節，使學生再也無法重溫題目或提出異議。他們所定之答案，即成最終答案，無從驗證真偽。此實為我平生所遇最惡劣之考試，五十題中僅確信二十一題，餘者皆須猜度。整個課程，實是一場自欺欺人的猜謎遊戲。我衷心不推薦任何人修讀，無論你的背景或興趣為何，因為他們將竭盡所能，摧毀你的一切熱情。
再者，此科雖是我最早考畢的一科，卻是最後一科收到成績的科目——而它僅包含選擇題。這再度證明了教學團隊的怠惰與無能，因這是我唯一完全無法申請覆核查卷的課程。至此，對其評級我已無話可說，惟因此科給了我本學期最差的成績。哈哈。
客觀而論，以我在此科投入的微薄努力（期中溫習三日，期末溫習四小時，得B+），此成績或許不算太壞（可悲的是，我大抵已是B+的最高分之一）。然而，實情是：即便投入更多時間溫習，我的分數也未必提升，此乃我親見期末試卷後的結論。我僅是幸運而已。亦不知是直覺抑或僥倖，我猜對了近半題目，然此「策略」恐難複製。坦率而言，我全然不知應如何為此科備考，故將其評為「E」——因努力與成績之間的關聯，在此科低得可憐。
若閣下欲測試自身運勢，歡迎一試。

Format and Grading Rules
Homework
Homework questions will be posted at the beginning of each chapter as self-learning materials. Students are not required to hand in homework solutions. Homework solutions will be provided by the instructors about one week after each chapter concludes.
Quizzes (iPRS)
Full marks for correct answers, 1/4 mark for incorrect answers, 0 mark for no answers.
The best 80% of a student’s quiz answers will be counted for the total marks of PRS and tutorial quizzes.
Marks of the PRS and MCQ quizzes conducted during the add-drop period will not be counted toward the final grade.
Late submissions or resubmissions will not be accepted.
MC and Strip-Sequence Quizzes
A strip-sequence question requires students to arrange a provided list of items in the correct order (not necessarily chronological). You can find sample questions posted in Canvas Files --> Sample Strip Sequence Questions. Points are awarded based on the number of inversions in the sequence on a linear scale, where full marks are given if all pairs are in the correct order, and zero marks are awarded if only half of the pairs are in the correct order.
For example, if a question presents 5 items, resulting in a total of 10 pairs, the marks will be allocated as follows:
Number of pairs in correct order | Marks
5 or fewer | 0%
6 | 20%
7 | 40%
8 | 60%
9 | 80%
10 | 100%
Student-Generated Question (SGQ)
Each student should generate ONE Multiple Choice (MC) question with FIVE choices (1 correct choice + 4 wrong choices) based on the contents of the lecture notes. You can find the marking scheme and two sample questions in Canvas Files --> Student-Generated Questions.
Written Report of an Open-ended Question (OEQ)
Each student has to submit an individual report and its topic must be chosen from one of the open-ended questions posted. You can find the report template and marking scheme in Canvas Files --> Open-Ended Questions --> Template and Marking Scheme.
Final Exam

comment_workload:
Fairly low. 
No weekly assignments. HW are provided for practice only, still useful for revision.
- 2 SGQ (Student Generated Questions):
Before the midterm and final, students are required to write a MC question, and each lecturer will pick one to include in the exam. Basic recall / Memorization questions is valued less than comprehensive quantitative questions (i.e. Calculation-based questions). You are required to explain your solution and include at least 1 distractor (an option that seems correct on the surface but isn't).
- iPRS (Attendance/Quiz):
Each class, there are a PRS quiz in the middle of the lecture and a MCQ at the end. Both of them are just an iPRS question related to that lecture's topic, not usually too difficult. Just that you will have to attend your registered lecture sessions.
Only the top 80% of your iPRS scores are counted, so you have some room for slip-ups or absences. 
As someone who attended 2 sessions, the iPRS questions are different between lecturers, so you may want to check out the other sessions' iPRS questions for revision in addition to your own.
- Cheat Sheet Making
Midterm allows 1 doubled-sided A4 cheat sheet; Final allows 3 doubled-sided A4 cheat sheets. There is a lot of stuff you need to consider to put in or not.
For the midterms, they explicitly said there will be questions requiring you to order things in specific sequence (e.g. Order events chronologically, order size of objects, etc...). Unless you want to memorize every little detail, which there are a lot of, you will have to find a way to fit them all in.
For the finals, less sequencing, but the later slides are really dense, so you need to read through them all and put the details in. Finding enough room is not much of a concern as the midterm, just that it takes a long time (especially if you have other courses' work piling on you). Took me a few days to make mine.
